limitations: Capacity figures are operator disclosures, not independent commissioning audits.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Hyperscalers have clearly been retrofitting old data centers to fit their new chips, and based on his research Zitron can find no compelling evidence that they have each added more than a few hundred megawatts since 2023.

statement.excerpt: Hyperscalers have clearly been retrofitting old data centers to fit their new chips, and based on my research, I can find no compelling evidence that they’ve added more than a few hundred megawatts a piece since 2023.
statement.document_title: Where Are All The Data Centers?

from_speaker: more than a few hundred megawatts a piece
our_interpretation: Assess the public evidence available by publication, not the private contents of Zitron's research.
Read since 2023 as January 1, 2023 through May 12, 2026. The cited capacity additions also fall after 2023, so the start-date ambiguity does not change the result.
The relevant major hyperscalers include AWS, Microsoft, and Google.
Retrofitting is a general practice claim, not an assertion that every facility was converted.
Added capacity means reported additions to available data center fleet capacity, including expansions and leased facilities. Future commitments and power-generation projects alone do not count.
No exact cutoff is assigned to a few hundred; multi-gigawatt additions plainly exceed it.
criteria.support_condition: Documented retrofits support the first component. A comprehensive review finding no credible per-provider additions clearly above a few hundred megawatts would support the second.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible pre-publication disclosures of realized gigawatt-scale additions by named hyperscalers contradict the claimed absence of compelling evidence. Planned additions alone do not.
